ANTI-DEFICIENCY PROTECTIONS AFTER FORECLOSURE OR SHORT SALE (CODE CIV. PROC. §§ 726, 580A, 580B, 580D, 580E) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 742 Oak St., Fresno, CA 93721 (APN 123-456-789) · Jordan Lee

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes what California law provides about deficiency judgments — the personal money judgment a lender may seek for the part of a debt that the sale of the real property security did not repay — as those rules may bear on the loan of Jordan Lee from Valley Coast Bank, N.A. secured by the real property at 742 Oak St., Fresno, CA 93721 (APN 123-456-789). It states what Code of Civil Procedure sections 726, 580a, 580b, 580d, and 580e and Civil Code section 2953 provide about the single-action and security-first requirements, the fair value limits on a deficiency after a judicial foreclosure sale, the absolute bar on a deficiency in purchase money transactions, the bar on a deficiency after a nonjudicial trustee's sale, and the bar on a deficiency after a lender-approved short sale of a dwelling of not more than four units. It also states what the California Supreme Court has held in Roseleaf Corp. v. Chierighino, Cornelison v. Kornbluth, Security Pacific National Bank v. Wozab, DeBerard Properties, Ltd. v. Lim, and Coker v. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. about how those statutes operate, when they may not be waived, what happens to a junior lienholder whose security is sold out by a senior sale, and what a full credit bid at a foreclosure sale does to a claim for waste. It does not determine whether any particular loan, sale, or claim involving 742 Oak St., Fresno, CA 93721 (APN 123-456-789) falls inside or outside any of these statutes, and it does not tell Jordan Lee or Valley Coast Bank, N.A. what to do.

THE ONE-FORM-OF-ACTION AND SECURITY-FIRST RULES OF CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE SECTION 726(A)
California's deficiency rules begin with Code of Civil Procedure section 726, subdivision (a), which provides that there can be but one form of action for the recovery of any debt or the enforcement of any right secured by mortgage upon real property or an estate for years therein, which action shall be in accordance with the provisions of that chapter, and that in the action the court may, by its judgment, direct the sale of the encumbered property and the application of the proceeds to the costs of court, the expenses of levy and sale, and the amount due the plaintiff, including a reasonable sum for attorney's fees where the mortgage provides for them, not exceeding the amount named in the mortgage. The California Supreme Court has described the two consequences the section carries. In Roseleaf Corp. v. Chierighino the court stated that, although a creditor secured by a trust deed or mortgage on real property could at common law realize the security or sue on the obligation or both, in California the creditor must rely upon his security before enforcing the debt. In Security Pacific National Bank v. Wozab the court restated the same idea in a single sentence: a secured creditor can bring only one lawsuit to enforce its security interest and collect its debt. Those two consequences are commonly called the one-form-of-action rule and the security-first rule.

WHAT HAPPENS WHEN A SECURED CREDITOR VIOLATES SECTION 726: WAIVER OF THE SECURITY, NOT FORFEITURE OF THE DEBT
Security Pacific National Bank v. Wozab describes what a violation of section 726 costs the creditor. The court stated the long-established rule that when a secured creditor violates section 726(a) by obtaining judgment on the debt before foreclosing upon the security, he is deemed to have waived the security, and applied that rule by parity of reasoning to a bank that had taken an extrajudicial setoff against its borrower's deposit account before exhausting its real property security. The court then declined to extend the sanction to the debt itself, framing the remaining issue as whether the bank's improper setoff required a forfeiture of the underlying debt and answering that the law does not require that draconian sanction. Reading its earlier decisions, the court observed that in those cases the creditors were allowed a judgment for the full amount of the debt and the only sanction was that the creditors lost their preferred position as secured creditors, in whole or in part, and were reduced to the status of unsecured creditors — which the court called a drastic sanction in the marketplace.

THE PURCHASE MONEY BAR OF CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE SECTION 580B
Code of Civil Procedure section 580b states an unconditional bar for purchase money transactions. Subdivision (a) provides that, except as provided in subdivision (c), no deficiency shall be owed or collected, and no deficiency judgment shall lie, in three situations: after a sale of real property or an estate for years therein for failure of the purchaser to complete his or her contract of sale; under a deed of trust or mortgage given to the vendor to secure payment of the balance of the purchase price of that real property or estate for years therein; and under a deed of trust or mortgage on a dwelling for not more than four families given to a lender to secure repayment of a loan that was used to pay all or part of the purchase price of that dwelling, occupied entirely or in part by the purchaser — a loan the statute calls a "purchase money loan." Subdivision (b) carries the bar into refinancing: no deficiency is owed or collected on a credit transaction used to refinance a purchase money loan, or on subsequent refinances of one, except to the extent the lender advances new principal that is not applied to the purchase money obligation or to the fees, costs, or related expenses of the credit transaction, and a new credit transaction is deemed a purchase money loan except as to the principal amount of a new advance. Subdivision (c) states the limit of the protection: the fact that no deficiency is owed or collected does not affect the liability a guarantor, pledgor, or other surety might otherwise have, or that might be satisfied from other collateral pledged to secure the obligation. Subdivision (d) extends the bar to a combined sale: where both a chattel mortgage and a deed of trust or mortgage secure the balance of the combined purchase price of real and personal property, no deficiency judgment lies under either if none would lie under the real property security.

THE PURPOSES THE SUPREME COURT HAS ASCRIBED TO THE PURCHASE MONEY BAR
The California Supreme Court explained the reasons for the purchase money bar in Roseleaf Corp. v. Chierighino. The court stated that section 580b places the risk of inadequate security on the purchase money mortgagee, that a vendor is thus discouraged from overvaluing the security, and that precarious land promotion schemes are discouraged because the security value of the land gives purchasers a clue as to its true market value. The court added a second, economy-wide reason: if inadequacy of the security results not from overvaluing but from a decline in property values during a general or local depression, section 580b prevents the aggravation of the downturn that would result if defaulting purchasers were burdened with large personal liability, so that the section serves as a stabilizing factor in land sales. Three decades later, in DeBerard Properties, Ltd. v. Lim, the court described the operative text as plain and summarized its effect in one sentence: a vendor is barred from obtaining a deficiency judgment against a purchaser in a purchase money secured land transaction.

WAIVER: CIVIL CODE SECTION 2953 AND THE SUPREME COURT ON WAIVING SECTION 580B
Two sources address agreements by which a borrower gives up these protections. Civil Code section 2953 provides that any express agreement made or entered into by a borrower at the time of or in connection with the making or renewing of a loan secured by a deed of trust, mortgage, or other instrument creating a lien on real property, whereby the borrower agrees to waive the rights or privileges conferred by Civil Code sections 2924, 2924b, or 2924c or by Code of Civil Procedure sections 580a or 726, shall be void and of no effect. Section 580b is not on that list, and in DeBerard Properties, Ltd. v. Lim the California Supreme Court held that its omission does not permit a waiver after the sale either: the court stated that it did not believe the Legislature's failure to cite section 580b in Civil Code section 2953 permits a post-sale waiver of antideficiency judgment protection, reasoning that the statute's strict language runs counter to the possibility of waiver, contemporaneous or subsequent. The court grounded that conclusion in the public character of the statute's purpose, stating that a key purpose of section 580b is to stabilize the state's economy, to the benefit of all, and that the public benefit section 580b provides is one of its primary purposes. In Coker v. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., the court applied the same principle to a borrower's promise, given in exchange for the lender's approval of a short sale, to remain liable for the shortfall, holding that the borrower could not validly waive section 580b's protection in exchange for that approval.

THE SHORT SALE BAR OF CODE OF CIVIL PROCEDURE SECTION 580E
Code of Civil Procedure section 580e addresses the lender-approved short sale. Subdivision (a)(1) provides that no deficiency shall be owed or collected, and no deficiency judgment requested or rendered, on a note secured solely by a deed of trust or mortgage for a dwelling of not more than four units where the trustor or mortgagor sells the dwelling for less than the remaining indebtedness in accordance with the written consent of the holder, provided that title has been voluntarily transferred to a buyer by grant deed or other recorded conveyance and the sale proceeds have been tendered to the mortgagee, beneficiary, or agent in accordance with the parties' agreement. Subdivision (b) provides that a holder shall not require the trustor, mortgagor, or maker of the note to pay any additional compensation, aside from the proceeds of the sale, in exchange for the written consent to the sale. Subdivision (c) preserves the holder's remedies for fraud or waste. Subdivision (d)(1) states that the section does not apply if the trustor or mortgagor is a corporation, limited liability company, limited partnership, or political subdivision of the state. Subdivision (e) provides that any purported waiver of subdivision (a) or (b) shall be void and against public policy.

COKER V. JPMORGAN CHASE BANK: SECTION 580B APPLIES TO SHORT SALES AS WELL AS FORECLOSURE SALES
Before section 580e existed, the question arose whether the purchase money bar of section 580b reached a short sale, in which the borrower rather than the lender sells the home. In Coker v. JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A., the California Supreme Court described a short sale as one in which the borrower sells the home to a third party for an amount that falls short of the outstanding loan balance, the lender agrees to release its lien on the property to facilitate the sale, and the borrower agrees to give all the proceeds to the lender; the court held that the statute applies to short sales just as it does to foreclosure sales. The court also addressed the relationship between the two statutes at issue in that case, stating that when a borrower waives her rights under section 726 by agreeing to a short sale, section 580b remains a barrier to any deficiency judgment after the lender collects the full value of its security from the sale.

The statute requires the plaintiff to set forth in the complaint the entire amount of the indebtedness secured at the time of sale, the amount for which the property was sold, its fair market value at the date of sale, and the date of that sale. On the application of either party made at least 10 days before trial the court must, and on its own motion may at any time, appoint a probate referee to appraise the property as of the time of sale, and the appraisal is admissible in evidence. Before rendering any judgment the court must find the fair market value of the property at the time of sale, and the statute caps the judgment at the amount by which the indebtedness due at the time of sale exceeded that fair market value, with a further cap: exclusive of post-sale interest, the judgment may not exceed the difference between the sale price and the entire secured indebtedness. The statute closes with a deadline and a security-first requirement of its own: any such action must be brought within three months of the time of sale, and no judgment may be rendered until the property has first been sold pursuant to the terms of the deed of trust or mortgage, unless the property has become valueless.

The California Supreme Court held that in situations arising under section 580d, recovery for waste against the mortgagor following a nonjudicial foreclosure sale is barred by the section's proscription against deficiency judgments when the waste actually results from the depressed condition of the general real estate market, but not when the waste is caused by the bad faith acts of the mortgagor. Cornelison also describes what the lender's own bid at the sale does to such a claim. The court noted that a foreclosing mortgagee is not required to open the bidding with a full credit bid but may bid whatever amount it thinks the property worth, and held that a mortgagee who bids less than the full amount of the obligation, and so acquires property worth less than that amount, has an impaired security and may recover waste damages in an amount not exceeding the difference between the amount of its bid and the full amount of the outstanding indebtedness immediately before the foreclosure sale. The converse follows from the same reasoning: a lender that bids the full amount owed has extinguished its lien and can show no impairment of security, which is why the plaintiff in Cornelison, who had bought the property at the trustee's sale with a full credit bid, could not recover for waste.
